#668. A surprising vitamin A discovery is changing what scientists know about vision

Scientists at Johns Hopkins University have uncovered a surprising role for a vitamin A derivative in the development of human vision. Their research reveals how this molecule works alongside thyroid hormones to help form the part of the eye responsible for our sharpest sight, challenging a scientific explanation that has stood for roughly 30 years.

The discovery centers on an unexpected transformation that occurs in the developing retina before birth. Certain cells that initially detect blue light appear to change into cells sensitive to red and green light, helping create the specialized arrangement needed for clear central vision.

Published in Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences, the findings could reshape scientists' understanding of how human eyes develop. They may also help advance research into future treatments for macular degeneration, glaucoma, and other conditions that cause vision loss.

"This is a key step toward understanding the inner workings of the center of the retina, a critical part of the eye and the first to fail in people with macular degeneration," said Robert J. Johnston Jr., an associate professor of biology at Johns Hopkins University who led the study. "By better understanding this region and developing organoids that mimic its function, we hope to one day grow and transplant these tissues to restore vision."

How Scientists Recreated the Developing Human Retina

To investigate how human vision forms, Johnston and his colleagues turned to an innovative laboratory technique they have helped develop over the past several years. Instead of relying entirely on animal experiments, they grew miniature versions of human retinal tissue called organoids.

These small clusters of cells, grown from fetal cells, reproduce important features of developing human tissue. By observing the retinal organoids over several months, the scientists could follow changes that would otherwise be extremely difficult to study during pregnancy.

Their attention focused on the foveola, a tiny region at the very center of the retina. The retina is the light-sensitive layer at the back of the eye that converts incoming light into signals the brain can interpret. Within it, the foveola plays an especially important role in detailed central vision, which allows people to read, recognize faces, and distinguish fine details.

Although the foveola occupies only a small fraction of the retina, it is involved in approximately 50% of human visual perception, according to the researchers.

The Surprising Secret Behind Sharp Human Vision

One of the keys to understanding the foveola is a group of specialized light-detecting cells called cones. Unlike rod cells, which are particularly important for seeing in dim light, cones support daytime vision and allow us to perceive color.

Humans have three types of cone cells, each most sensitive to different wavelengths of light. These are commonly described as blue, green, and red cones. By comparing signals from these different cells, the brain can distinguish a remarkably broad range of colors.

However, the cones are not distributed evenly throughout the retina. The foveola contains red and green cones but lacks blue cones, which are found in other retinal regions. This precise arrangement is essential for the exceptionally sharp vision produced by the center of the eye.

For decades, researchers have struggled to explain how this pattern develops. One major obstacle is that commonly studied animals, including mice and fish, do not share the same retinal organization found in humans. That makes it difficult to use traditional animal models to investigate how these specialized cells develop.

The laboratory-grown human retinas offered a new opportunity to solve this longstanding mystery.

Vitamin A and Thyroid Hormones Trigger a Remarkable Change

The researchers discovered evidence that the arrangement of cones in the foveola develops through two coordinated processes. Together, they determine which types of cells form in the central retina and how some of those cells change as development continues.

During weeks 10 through 12 of fetal development, a small number of blue cones are initially present in the foveola. By week 14, however, these cells appear to have transformed into red and green cones.

The team identified two important chemical influences behind this process.

The first involves retinoic acid, a molecule produced from vitamin A. Retinoic acid helps regulate how cells develop and specialize throughout the body. In the developing retina, the breakdown of this molecule limits the formation of blue cones in the central region.

The second influence comes from thyroid hormones, which are best known for regulating metabolism but also have crucial roles in growth and development. In this case, the hormones appear to encourage the remaining blue cones to change into red and green cones.

"First, retinoic acid helps set the pattern. Then, thyroid hormone plays a role in converting the leftover cells," Johnston said. "That's very important because if you have those blue cones in there, you don't see as well."

Importantly, the discovery concerns how vitamin A signaling helps guide eye development before birth. It does not establish that taking vitamin A supplements can improve sharp vision in adults.

A Discovery That Challenges a 30-Year-Old Theory

The results offer a striking alternative to an explanation that has influenced vision research for decades.

Under the longstanding model, blue cones that initially appear in the foveola were thought to move away as the retina developed. Scientists generally assumed that once these cells became a particular type of cone, their identities remained fixed.

The new findings suggest something different. Rather than simply relocating, at least some blue cones may undergo a change in identity, becoming red or green cones as the eye develops.

"The main model in the field from about 30 years ago was that somehow the few blue cones you get in that region just move out of the way, that these cells decide what they're going to be, and they remain this type of cell forever," Johnston said. "We can't really rule that out yet, but our data supports a different model. These cells actually convert over time, which is really surprising."

The researchers have not completely ruled out the possibility that some cells migrate. Nevertheless, their observations support the idea that developing cone cells have more flexibility than previously recognized.

That possibility could fundamentally change how scientists study the formation of human color vision and the development of the retina's most specialized regions.

Could the Discovery Help Scientists Restore Lost Vision?

Beyond explaining how healthy eyes develop, the findings could have important implications for treating diseases that damage the retina.

One particularly promising application involves macular degeneration, a major cause of central vision loss, especially among older adults. The disease damages the macula, the retinal region responsible for detailed central vision, and can severely interfere with reading, driving, and recognizing faces. Although treatments can slow or manage certain forms of the disease, there is currently no cure.

Understanding how the retina creates its specialized light-sensitive cells could eventually help scientists produce healthy replacements in the laboratory.

Johnston's team is now working to improve its retinal organoids so they more closely reproduce the structure and function of the human eye. The long-term goal is to develop precisely controlled populations of photoreceptors, the cells that detect light, for potential transplantation into damaged retinas.

Katarzyna Hussey, a study author and former doctoral student in Johnston's laboratory, believes this approach could open an important new direction for vision restoration. Hussey is now a molecular and cell biologist at CiRC Biosciences, a cell therapy company in Chicago.

"The goal with using this organoid tech is to eventually make an almost made-to-order population of photoreceptors. A big avenue of potential is cell replacement therapy to introduce healthy cells that can reintegrate into the eye and potentially restore that lost vision," said Hussey.

The idea is to introduce healthy cells that could integrate with existing retinal tissue and potentially replace functions lost to disease. Achieving that goal would require researchers to demonstrate that transplanted cells can survive, connect properly with the eye's existing circuitry, and function safely.

Hussey emphasized that the technology remains far from routine clinical use, with extensive development and testing still necessary.

"These are very long-term experiments, and of course we'd need to do optimizations for safety and efficacy studies prior to moving into the clinic. But it's a viable journey."

For now, the discovery provides something fundamental: a clearer explanation of how the human eye develops its remarkable ability to see fine details. By revealing how vitamin A signaling and thyroid hormones help shape the retina, scientists have taken another step toward understanding vision at its earliest stages and potentially finding ways to restore it when disease strikes.

#667. Hubble reveals a stunning twist in how the universe emerged from darkness

A surprising discovery made with NASA's Hubble Space Telescope is challenging a leading explanation for how the early universe emerged from darkness. The findings suggest that powerful explosions from dying stars may have actually interfered with a process scientists once believed they helped drive.

An international research team, including astronomers from the University of Michigan, found that powerful winds produced by exploding stars can prevent ultraviolet radiation from escaping galaxies. This is the opposite of what a widely accepted theory had predicted, and it could change how scientists understand one of the most important transformations in cosmic history.

The discovery, published in Nature Astronomy, offers new clues about how the universe became transparent to ultraviolet light roughly 13 billion years ago.

How the Early Universe Emerged From Its Cosmic Fog

During the first billion years after the Big Bang, vast amounts of neutral hydrogen filled the space between galaxies. This hydrogen formed a kind of cosmic fog that absorbed ultraviolet radiation, preventing that light from traveling freely across the universe.

That changed during a period known as reionization, which began approximately 13 billion years ago. Intense radiation from early galaxies gradually transformed the hydrogen by stripping electrons from its atoms, leaving behind positively charged protons and free electrons.

As more hydrogen became ionized, ultraviolet light could travel much farther through intergalactic space. This transformation helped establish the relatively transparent universe that astronomers observe today.

"Eventually, when it ionized the majority of hydrogen filling intergalactic space, that was the end of reionization and we see the universe today," said Cody Carr, a postdoctoral researcher in the University of Michigan's Department of Astronomy. "We call reionization the last major phase transition of the universe."

Despite its enormous importance, astronomers still do not fully understand which objects supplied the radiation responsible for reionization or how enough of that radiation managed to escape from early galaxies.

"We don't know exactly what objects caused reionization or how it evolved," said Carr, who conducted and led the research while working as a postdoctoral scholar at Zhejiang University in China, before joining the University of Michigan. "We know that it took place, but we don't have complete answers to those questions."

Hubble Challenges a Leading Theory About Exploding Stars

For years, one prominent explanation centered on supernovae, the powerful explosions that occur when certain stars reach the ends of their lives. These explosions can generate enormous winds that sweep through galaxies, pushing gas and other material outward.

Scientists proposed that these winds cleared pathways through the gas surrounding young stars, allowing ultraviolet radiation to escape into the space between galaxies. Once outside, that radiation could help break apart the neutral hydrogen responsible for the universe's ancient fog.

However, new observations from Hubble suggest that this explanation may have the process backward.

Rather than opening routes for radiation to escape, the researchers found that stronger galactic winds were associated with less escaping ionizing radiation. The observations indicate that the winds generated by supernovae can actually make it harder for the radiation to leave a galaxy.

"Basically, how these galaxies were leaking ionizing radiation isn't what we thought," Carr said.

The results lend support to a different possibility. Radiation from young, massive stars may escape their galaxies before those stars explode as supernovae and generate large winds that reshape the surrounding environment.

"Our observations show that these photons are escaping before galactic winds form," Carr said.

Photons are individual packets of light energy. In this case, the researchers are interested in ultraviolet photons energetic enough to ionize hydrogen, making them essential to understanding how the early universe became transparent.

What Hubble Discovered in Nearby Starburst Galaxies

To investigate how radiation escapes, the international team used the Hubble Space Telescope to examine nearby starburst galaxies. These are galaxies experiencing exceptionally intense periods of star formation, making them useful modern examples of the kinds of galaxies believed to have contributed to reionization.

Hubble, a NASA mission launched with contributions from the European Space Agency, allowed researchers to study the light coming from these galaxies in detail.

The team examined their spectra, which reveal how much light is present at different wavelengths. By studying the patterns in those spectra, astronomers can learn about the gas surrounding stars and determine how quickly it is moving.

Gas absorbs particular wavelengths of light, creating recognizable dips in a galaxy's spectrum. The locations and shapes of these dips provide clues about the speed and movement of galactic winds.

When the researchers compared wind speeds with the amount of ionizing radiation escaping from each galaxy, they uncovered a surprising relationship. Galaxies with the fastest winds allowed the smallest fraction of ionizing radiation to escape.

That result directly challenges the expectation that stronger winds should clear away more gas and make it easier for radiation to reach intergalactic space.

"It appears that energy input from supernovae has stirred up the surroundings and increased, rather than decreased, the coverage of neutral gas and dust that suppresses ionizing radiation escape," said Stephan McCandliss, a senior author of the study and director of the Center for Astrophysical Sciences at Johns Hopkins University.

In other words, instead of clearing a path for ultraviolet light, energy from exploding stars appears to redistribute gas and dust in ways that can block more of it.

Young Stars May Hold the Key to Cosmic Reionization

Although large galactic winds appear to suppress escaping radiation, smaller winds and other activity around young stars could still help create openings in the surrounding gas.

These processes may occur before the first supernova explosions, giving radiation a chance to escape while conditions are more favorable.

The findings suggest that astronomers may need to pay greater attention to what happens during the earliest stages of star formation, rather than focusing primarily on the effects of exploding stars.

Carr and his colleagues are seeking additional observing time with Hubble to examine more galaxies and investigate whether the same patterns appear elsewhere. More observations could help establish how important the activity of young stars is in allowing ionizing radiation to escape.

The results also have implications for computer simulations of the early universe. These simulations attempt to recreate how galaxies formed, how gas moved through them, and how radiation eventually transformed the hydrogen filling intergalactic space.

"Supernovae play a central role in cosmological hydrodynamic simulations that explain how ionizing radiation escapes from galaxies," said Renyue Cen, a senior author of the study and professor and director of the Center for Cosmology and Computational Astrophysics at Zhejiang University. "Our findings highlight the need to examine how radiation and winds from young stars shape the surrounding gas before the first supernovae explode."

By accounting more accurately for these early interactions between stars, radiation, and gas, researchers may be able to build better models of how reionization unfolded.

The discovery does not yet settle the question of what caused the universe's last major phase transition. However, it provides an important new clue, suggesting that the radiation that helped lift the universe's ancient fog may have escaped galaxies before powerful stellar explosions began to alter their surroundings.

International Research Collaboration and Funding

The research brought together nearly 30 scientists from more than a dozen institutions around the world. Sally Oey, a professor of astronomy at the University of Michigan, also contributed to the study.

The project received additional financial support from Zhejiang University, the Zhejiang Provincial Top-Level Research Support Program, the National Natural Science Foundation of China, the Ministry of Science, Innovation and Universities in Spain, the European Regional Development Fund, and the European Union's Horizon 2020 Research and Innovation Program.

The research was also supported in part by federal funding from NASA and the U.S. National Science Foundation. Additional support for the Hubble Space Telescope observations came through a grant administered by the Space Telescope Science Institute.

#666. The dachshund, a humorous icon with political symbolism

From Picasso to Andy Warhol, a surprising number of artists have portrayed the German breed. But the dachshund has also at times been co-opted as a political symbol.

Pablo Picasso was renowned for having numerous muses — mostly women with whom he also had harmful relationships. But there's at least one of these muses who was freed from toxic romantic entanglement: a cute dachshund called Lump.

Before becoming his most famous canine model, Lump originally belonged to US photojournalist David Douglas Duncan.

The dog and the photographer visited Picasso at his villa in Cannes in 1967. According to Duncan, upon their first encounter, Lump jumped right onto Picasso's lap. He apparently "decided" to stay with the painter, and they lived together for six years.

The story does not reveal how Lump's decision was communicated, but that immediate special bound was immortalized through art: Picasso painted the dachshund's portrait directly onto a ceramic dinner plate that day, and Duncan did a series of photos documenting them together while the work was created.

The plate and the photos are on show at the new exhibition "The Dachshund. An Icon off the Leash" held at the Kunsthalle Bremen until March 28, 2027.

Lump also appears in many of Picasso's series of paintings reinterpreting Diego Velazquez's masterwork "Las Meninas," in which the original work's large mastiff was replaced with Picasso's adoptive pet.

With their long ears and extreme length compared to their short legs, dachshunds have a silhouette that's instantly recognizable: "It's really a dog with an iconic shape, and that makes them interesting for many things" — from art to advertisement, says exhibition curator and art historian Annett Reckert.

Alongside Picasso, a surprising number of important artists, including Andy Warhol, Otto Dix, David Hockney, Max Liebermann and Rosemarie Trockel, have paid tribute to the dachshund. "It's striking how often the dachshund has served as a muse, model and studio accomplice for them," Reckert tells DW.

Combined with this prolific artistic career, the dachshund can equally be explored from a historical perspective, since "there's also the fact that we associate them with something German," the curator adds.

Bred to track and chase badgers, foxes, rabbits and other burrowing animals, the dachshund originated in Germany over 300 years ago. Breed standards were established in 1879, and the German Teckel Club (DTK) — one of the oldest dog breeding organizations in Germany — was founded in 1888.

The name combines the German words "Dachs" (badger) and "Hund" (dog), literally translating to "badger dog." But Germans more commonly call them Dackel or Teckel.

Because of their long, narrow build, dachshunds are also colloquially known in English-speaking countries as wiener dogs or sausage dogs.

Beyond their role as hunting dogs, dachshunds have a surprisingly rich place in German cultural history, from bourgeois stereotype to Olympic icon.

Germany's last emperor, Kaiser Wilhelm II, was an avid dachshund enthusiast and owned several of them.

Two of his dogs, Wadl and Hexlsome, made history by causing a minor diplomatic incident during a visit to the estate of Archduke Franz Ferdinand, Konopiste Castle, in 1908. The dachshunds reportedly killed one of the archduke's prized golden pheasants. The attack was widely commented on in aristocratic circles, and Kaiser Wilhelm II was forced to issue a formal apology.

The pheasant incident was obviously not as consequential as another event involving Franz Ferdinand, heir to the Austro-Hungarian throne: his assassination in Sarajevo on June 28, 1914, which became the primary catalyst of World War I.

Still, the dachshund remained present throughout this global conflict. In propaganda maps and political cartoons, Germany was represented as a dachshund, the British as a bulldog and the French, a poodle.

The popularity of the dachshund in the United States plummeted during the World War I because of this association; those who owned one called their dogs "liberty hounds" instead of using the German word.

During World War II, dachshunds were used for military tasks such as mine detection.

However, their missions weren't as outlandish as the stories published by the UK's tabloid press relatively recently, which claimed that the Nazis aimed to build armies of talking dachshunds. The rumors followed the publication of a non-fiction book on dogs published in 2011, "Amazing Dogs: A Cabinet of Canine Curiosities," which outlined Nazi research into dogs' — including dachshunds' — intelligence and personalities.

The dachshund definitely didn't fit into the Nazis' aesthetics: "They were used in the war, too, but not in the same way as other dogs. After all, they weren't the kind of dog a Nazi would have wanted to be seen with for the sake of appearances," notes Reckert. "Take Hitler, for instance: He famously made public appearances with his German Shepherd, Blondie. They would rather be seen with a Doberman or dogs that looked big and dangerous."

The endearing potential of the dachshund is actually one of the ideas that guided Reckert in her curation of the exhibition. They "simply give the impression that they have a sense of humor," the art historian says. "That's an attribution, of course. But they really do spread good cheer and have a truly likable character."

In the 1970s, this slightly absurd and cheerful domestic companion inspired a figure embodying a new image for West Germany: the official mascot for the 1972 Summer Olympics in Munich, Waldi.

A stark contrast to the heavy symbols that represented Germany during the Third Reich — the eagle, Germania, forests, Wagner and Prussian discipline — the mascot created by renowned graphic designer Otl Aicher and his intern, Elena Schwaiger, was as iconic as the shape of the dachshund.

The designer was vehemently against including brown or any of Germany's national colors — red, black and gold — in the brand identity. Instead, he went for delicate pastel shades: "The approach to color was truly visionary," notes Reckert. "Their intention was something we are still working on today — something we still haven't completely achieved: an open, cheerful, democratic and colorful Germany."

Still today, right-wing extremist groups attempt to co-opt the dachshund as a subtle nationalist fashion symbol that appears on ties or socks, inspired by accessories worn by Alexander Gauland. On the other hand, "Dachshunds Against the Right" has also emerged as a counter-protest movement.

But altogether, Reckert has focused on the dachshund as a symbol of friendliness and joy while conceiving "The Dachshund. An Icon off the Leash." The exhibition includes halls that are open to small dogs and even features artworks and performances specifically designed for them.

The feedback Reckert's been getting in the run-up to the show also aligns with this cheerful image. She notes that hardly a day goes by without something arriving in the mail related to the dachshund — whether pictures, artworks or information about dachshund-related events.

"It's really crazy," she says, showing examples of the stuff she's received. "I've never had an exhibition that was greeted ahead of its opening in such a friendly, diverse way. It's almost a bit uncanny, really."

NASA's Artemis IV moon mission will be a complicated affair — especially if SpaceX's Starship ends up being the lunar lander.

For all of the changing components of the Artemis program over the past several years, one of its most persistent may be the question of how many refueling flights Starship will need to land astronauts on the moon.

By summer 2021, it was common knowledge that Starship would require multiple launches to pull off an Artemis moon landing. A Government Accountability Office audit at the time, for example, estimated that it could take up to 16.

Earlier this month, a member of the Aerospace Safety Advisory Panel said the refueling number could be as high as 22. But that estimate was quickly refuted by SpaceX founder and CEO Elon Musk, who posted on his social media platform, X, that it would actually be closer to six or eight.

Perhaps an even bigger head scratcher, though, is how the refueling process will be carried out. Where (and when) will Starship's upper stage gas up when it's off planet? NASA released a graphic during a recent Artemis update that outlined an order of operations for the spacecraft on Artemis IV, which will be the program's first crewed lunar landing.

The mission will launch a Space Launch System (SLS) rocket with the four Artemis IV astronauts aboard NASA's Orion capsule to high Earth orbit, where they will rendezvous and dock with the Starship lunar lander.

Using Starship's engines, the two spacecraft will burn for the moon, and separate upon their arrival in low lunar orbit. Two astronauts will remain aboard Orion, while the other two will head down to the lunar surface in Starship.

After a little run through the regolith and a celebration of America's triumphant return to the moon, the duo will board Starship again to launch back to lunar orbit and dock with Orion before beginning the trip back to Earth.

All that seems well and good for a mission to the moon, and even has some resemblances with missions from NASA's Apollo days. What doesn't seem as immediately obvious when mapping out the Artemis IV mission outline, though, are the steps that Starship will be taking during its refueling process before the astronauts ever make it to space.

Orion will rendezvous with Starship in high Earth orbit — but that's not where the lander will launch initially. According to NASA's Artemis IV outline, SpaceX will first launch a depot ship to low Earth orbit (LEO), which will serve as the repository for all the fuel the Starship lander will eventually need.

The graphic shows a tanker Starship docked with the depot with "(multiple)" written next to it, so we don't know how many refueling flights will be needed for this initial depot fill. Once that's done, SpaceX will launch the Starship lunar lander to join the depot in LEO for its first pit stop.

Then, and this is where some of the head scratching begins, Starship will undock from the depot and raise its altitude to what NASA has labeled the "final tanking orbit," or FTO.

At some point after the Starship lander departs LEO, SpaceX will launch another round of "(multiple)" tanker ships to fill the depot with even more propellant. It will apparently then send the depot to meet the lander for another refill in FTO, where, as the name suggests, the two will dock for the pair's final fuel transfer.

After bidding the depot a second farewell, Starship will ascend to high Earth orbit to meet Orion.

NASA's graphic shows SLS launching Orion before Starship gets the last of its fuel, and the agency's website explainer for Artemis IV says the unusually choreographed order of operations for the mission does serve a purpose.

However many fuel boosts Starship ends up needing to get from LEO to the surface of the moon, its staggered orbital staging will apparently create some flexibility around when SLS can launch the Artemis IV astronauts to begin their mission.

And while Starship's orbital dance seems unnecessarily complicated, NASA says the new approach will actually reduce the amount of fuel SpaceX needs for the mission.

That's partly because Starship will take Orion directly to low lunar orbit, instead of the much higher orbit envisioned in previous mission plans.

But keep in mind: None of this is set in stone. If SpaceX can't demonstrate that its orbital refueling strategy works, or if it can't pull off an uncrewed lunar landing mission by the end of next year, NASA could still select Blue Origin's Blue Moon lander for Artemis IV — assuming Blue Moon is able to check its required boxes in time. Regardless of which company's lander delivers the first Artemis astronauts to the moon's surface, exactly how the pieces of those missions will come together should become clearer as the launch date gets closer. So, while SpaceX's refueling remains an open one for the time being, it's one of many for which we'll soon have an answer.

Josh Dinner is Space.com's Spaceflight Staff Writer and a photographer with a passion for science and exploration. He has worked the space beat since 2016, covering the evolution of NASA's commercial spaceflight partnerships and crewed missions, planetary science missions, the Artemis program and humanity's return to the moon. He also enjoys building 1:144-scale model rockets and spacecraft. Find some of Josh's launch photography on Instagram, and follow him on X, where he mostly posts in haiku.

#664. Scientists reveal a hidden snakebite crisis killing up to 513,000 people a year

Not every snakebite injects venom. When venom enters the body, however, it can cause snake envenoming. This is a potentially fatal condition and it mostly affects poor rural communities across tropical and subtropical regions who don’t have easy access to medical care.

As researchers with decades of combined experience in snakebite and tropical disease epidemiology, we came to realise that snake envenoming faces a data crisis. Over half of the countries where venomous snakes pose a threat don’t keep count of how many people are bitten or envenomed.

In rural sub-Saharan Africa and south Asia, many victims live hours away from the nearest clinic, lack transport, or seek care from traditional healers. As a result, their cases are never captured in national health statistics.

To bridge this massive gap, we conducted a study to map the global burden of snake envenoming and related deaths.

We looked at data from 79 countries by reviewing studies published up to March 31, 2025. This allowed us to update the findings from our milestone 2008 global burden study. To fill the remaining data gaps, we built a geostatistical model that combines real-world data with local environmental and socioeconomic factors. This allowed us to estimate envenoming and fatality rates.

We conclude from our findings that snake envenoming is a public health crisis on a far greater scale than official statistics have shown. Our results show that sub-Saharan Africa bears the heaviest toll.

The World Health Organization has set an ambitious target to halve snakebite mortality and disability by 2030. Mapping the problem at the country level is the first crucial step.

To overcome the lack of reliable data, we turned to a model-based geostatistics framework.

To understand how this modelling works, think of it as predicting invisible patterns by combining known data points with environmental signals. Instead of assuming data for every region, this modelling uses statistical probability to calculate a range of likely outcomes based on environmental signals.

We fed our model with data including climate, snake species richness and socioeconomic indicators. The model then calculated the probability of snakebites occurring in specific locations, even where official health records were completely blank.

By comparing different data sources (including hospital-reported data and regional statistics) against ground level community-survey data, our framework allowed us to account for unreported snake envenomings. It produced both a baseline floor and a potential upper ceiling for snake envenomings and fatalities.

Based on this, we estimate that at least 2.1 million people experience snake envenoming each year globally. The true number could be high as 7 million. Using our model, which adjusts for substantial under-reporting, annual deaths may range from 274,000 to 513,000.

The geographic distribution of this burden is uneven. Our research shows that sub-Saharan Africa alone accounts for 45% of all global envenomings and fatalities. That burden has likely been underestimated for decades. People in sub-Saharan Africa experience snake envenoming and death at nearly three times the rate seen in south Asia.

Countries like Nigeria, the Democratic Republic of Congo and Ethiopia face a high burden, driven by dense rural populations and high exposure in agricultural fields.

The reasons sub-Saharan Africa suffers such disproportionate harm are structural rather than accidental.

Firstly, the continent hosts a rich diversity of medically important venomous species. These include saw-scaled vipers (Echis spp.), puff adders (Bitis arietans), African cobras (Naja spp.) and mambas (Dendroaspis spp.). They are responsible for substantial morbidity and mortality across the continent.

Secondly, millions of rural agricultural workers labor in open fields without protective boots and walk on unlit footpaths at night. When a bite occurs, fragile health systems, long travel distances to regional facilities and the high cost or total absence of effective antivenom mean a treatable medical emergency can quickly become fatal. Similar conditions exist in parts of Asia.

We estimate that over 800,000 survivors are left with long-term physical disabilities each year, including amputations and other permanent impairments. These disabilities can reduce household income, increase healthcare costs and push already vulnerable farming families deeper into poverty.

Meeting the World Health Organization’s goal requires moving away from guesswork and using spatial risk data to guide real-world policy.

By identifying high-risk hotspots, governments and global health partners can strategically stockpile antivenom where it is needed most, train primary healthcare workers in high-burden rural zones and improve rapid transport infrastructure.

Snake envenoming has remained hidden for too long. Better data cannot solve the problem, but can help ensure that antivenom, healthcare services and prevention efforts reach the communities that need them most.

The Times credits associate puzzle editor Wyna Liu with helping to create the new word game and bringing it to the publications' Games section. Connections can be played on both web browsers and mobile devices and require players to group four words that share something in common.

Each puzzle features 16 words and each grouping of words is split into four categories. These sets could comprise of anything from book titles, software, country names, etc. Even though multiple words will seem like they fit together, there's only one correct answer.

If a player gets all four words in a set correct, those words are removed from the board. Guess wrong and it counts as a mistake—players get up to four mistakes until the game ends.

Players can also rearrange and shuffle the board to make spotting connections easier. Additionally, each group is color-coded with yellow being the easiest, followed by green, blue, and purple. Like Wordle, you can share the results with your friends on social media.

#662. Scientists discover mysterious seahorse lookalikes that no one has ever seen alive

At first glance it looks exactly like a seahorse. It has the same horse-shaped head tilted down from the body, the same curled and grasping tail, and in the males a fully enclosed pouch for brooding the young.

But this little fish, no longer than your thumb, is not a seahorse, as we report in our new study published in the Journal of Lost Species. This is Australyichthys aegis, a newly described fish from the deep reefs off southern Australia. We have given it the common name helmethead sea muppet, after the domed, helmet-like crest on its head.

Its scientific name follows the same idea: in Greek mythology the aegis was a protective shield. Together with its two relatives, the bullneck sea muppet (A. minotaur) and the paradoxical sea muppet (A. paradoxus), it makes up a small group we nickname the sea muppets.

All three, we have now shown, belong on their own branch of the family tree. The seahorse look has arisen more than once, and these fish are a case of it evolving well away from the true seahorses. That evidence had been sitting in museum drawers, misfiled, for decades.

You will not find these fish while scuba diving.

Every known specimen was brought up by accident, caught in trawl nets or dredges working the seafloor between about 50 and 125 meters down. The single specimen of A. aegis came up in 2006 near the Gambier Islands, at the mouth of South Australia’s Spencer Gulf.

The dredge that caught it was sampling for small shelled animals known as brachiopods during a natural history expedition. Because that expedition was after invertebrates, the fish was mistakenly catalogued into the invertebrate collection of the South Australian Museum, where it sat unrecognized for years.

After each chance capture the fish were preserved, then largely forgotten. The rest are held in Australian museum collections, among them the Australian Museum, Museums Victoria and CSIRO.

The whole genus is known from just seven specimens gathered over about 65 years, scattered across more than 2,500 kilometers of coastline, and nothing has been collected in nearly two decades.

The specimens are irreplaceable, so we could not dissect them. Instead we used micro-CT scanning, the same X-ray technology used in hospitals but fine enough to resolve tiny bones.

That let us build three-dimensional models of each fish’s skeleton and compare them bone by bone with true seahorses (Hippocampus).

Every earlier assessment had rested on external appearance, and the skeletons did not support it. Seahorses have a particular internal architecture, including a rigid cage of fused bony plates supporting the belly and a bony crown, called a coronet, on the head.

Our scans showed that Australyichthys has neither. In their place is a different arrangement of bones supporting the belly, one that appears in no seahorse.

A. aegis had been fixed in ethanol rather than formalin, the only member of the genus stored that way, and ethanol leaves genetic material intact. Sequencing it placed the fish well outside the seahorses, on the branch that is their closest relative. The genes said what the bones had already said.

All three species had been placed in the seahorse genus on the strength of how they look, and on that evidence they were seahorses. They are not, and they needed a genus of their own. We named it Australyichthys, from the Latin for southern and the Greek for fish.

When separate lineages evolve to look alike, biologists call it convergent evolution, and it usually reflects a shared way of life rather than shared ancestry.

The whole seahorse body, with its bent head, gripping tail and brood pouch, has been built at least twice within a single fish family, the Syngnathidae, which includes seahorses, pipefishes, pipehorses and seadragons.

Working out how that happened may reveal why evolution keeps arriving at the same solution.

All this happened along the Great Southern Reef, the connected system of kelp forests and rocky reefs that rings southern Australia. Many of its species are found nowhere else, and its deeper zones are barely explored.

In fact, an entire genus of vertebrate hid there, misidentified, until a CT scanner settled the question.

No one has ever seen one of these fish alive; they have turned up only by chance in a passing net or dredge. On that record they now qualify as lost species, known from a handful of preserved animals and never from a living one.

Calling them lost is not a prediction of extinction. It marks them as a priority for targeted surveys that go looking rather than waiting for the next accidental catch. They are most likely still down there, in a part of the sea we hardly ever visit.

A tiny robot cube is zipping around the International Space Station, trying to help astronauts with the endless challenging tasks onboard.

Reminiscent of Rocky rolling around the lab helping out Dr. Ryland Grace in Project Hail Mary, the Astrobee robot is a helpful assistant for astronauts aboard the space station.

A metal cube about the size of a toaster, the Astrobees are free-flying robotic assistants that NASA developed to help out astronauts. The first two Astrobee robots (named Bumble and Honey) were sent to the station in 2019. The third Astrobee robot, named Queen, joined later that year, and 7 years later, the program is still going strong.

So what can a free-floating cube help with? The robots are designed to assist the astronauts onboard with testing new technologies in microgravity and helping mission team members back on Earth to better observe inside the station. The little robot cubes can even help astronauts with everyday chores in space.

In this image, snapped by NASA astronaut and Crew-13 commander Jessica Watkins, we can see one of the Astrobee robots helping out in the station's Kibo laboratory.

The idea of a robot assistant helping out with chores and technology development aboard an orbiting space laboratory sounds positively science fiction.

While Astrobee is certainly not the first robot in space or aboard the space station, its compact shape and ability to fly autonomously gives it a unique quality. It really looks like a companion aboard the space station.

While the robotic space helpers of today might be cute little cubes, the success of the Astrobee program begs the question of how robots in space might continue to evolve. Will astronauts on the moon have robotic companions autonomously exploring and helping out? What will they look like?

Chelsea Gohd served as a Senior Writer for Space.com from 2018 to 2022 before returning in 2026, covering everything from climate change to planetary science and human spaceflight in both articles and on-camera in videos. With a M.S. in Biology, Chelsea has written and worked for institutions including NASA JPL, the American Museum of Natural History, Scientific American, Discover Magazine Blog, Astronomy Magazine, and Live Science. #660. Many Turkish 'guest workers' hit by poverty in old age

West Germany and Turkey signed an agreement allowing the temporary recruitment of workers on October 30, 1961. Sixty-five years on, many so-called 'guest workers' can't live from their pensions.

Düsseldorf Airport is a historically symbolic location. This is where the first Turkish "guest workers," as they were called at the time in Germany, arrived 65 years ago.

At a ceremony there in in mid-September, North Rhine-Westphalia's premier, Henrik Wüst, commemorated the courage of this first generation of migrants and their contribution to Germany's prosperity.

By the time recruitment ended in 1973, some 870,000 Turkish men and women had migrated to Germany for work. They toiled in the coal mines, did piecework on assembly lines or cleaned factory floors. Most settled in Düsseldorf, Cologne or Duisburg. "They have made our country more diverse, more open and stronger," said Wüst. However, he also stressed: "We will have reached our goal only once name, skin color and religion no longer matter."

According to integration expert Haci-Halil Uslucan, Germany is still a long way from that.

Even 65 years later, he told DW, people of Turkish descent still suffer a great deal of discrimination in Germany.

But he believes that the German Turkish labor recruitment agreement was, in the main, a success story.

"We've seen success in many areas, such as education. Today, we have a large number of college graduates, and we've seen professional advancement. And successful political careers. Take Baden-Württemberg's state premier, Cem Özdemir, for example," he said.

Uslucan himself is one such a success story. His father came to Berlin from Turkey and worked in the textile industry. Two years later, his father brought his wife and two sons to join him in Germany.

Haci-Halil Uslucan subsequently earned his Ph.D. in psychology and a professor of contemporary Turkish studies at the University of Duiburg-Essen.

One of his most recent research topics addresses the dark side of the labor recruitment agreement. He is examining loneliness, an issue that affects and troubles many former so-called "guest workers."

But poverty is also increasingly taking its toll on some people of Turkish descent reaching retirement age.

With a rate of between 25-30%, poverty in old age is twice as high among migrants in Germany than among Germans, which is about 12-14%, he says, adding that the disability rate and the rate of early retirement are significantly higher among migrants because the first generation did very heavy physical labor.

They are also twice as likely to become unemployed 10 years before reaching retirement age, says Uslucan.

"In addition, their monthly income is lower, they are more likely to have had employment gaps and worked in low-wage sectors. As a result, their pensions are also low."

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

An analysis by Germany's pension insurance fund (DRV) for the Mediendienst Integration, an information service for journalists on migration topics, uncovered some alarming figures: In Germany, pensioners with Turkish citizenship receive, on average, about €890 ($997) in pension benefits per month. That is €360 less than German pensioners, who receive €1,250 per month on average.

Even more troubling is that in June 2026, more than three times as many retirees with Turkish citizenship relied on top-up welfare benefits as Germans (9.3% compared to 2.7%).

One reason for this is that many of the Turkish workers who came to Germany were already in the middle of their working lives and consequently has less years to contribute to their pension fund, social scientist Eric Seils of the Hans Böckler Foundation in Düsseldorf told DW.

"But, of course, the most important reason is that they earned less in wages and had a shorter work history. The guest workers who came to Germany often went straight to factories, mines or construction sites. There, they didn't earn high hourly wages because they were often less educated than the Germans," he added.

With deindustrialization in the early 1970s and the oil crisis, many Turkish workers in Germany also lost their jobs.

"There weren't as many good jobs available at traditional industrial companies. Those who weren't as well-educated were more likely to become unemployed than those with an education — and the same was true for Germans. And when working lives are interrupted, that naturally has an impact on retirement benefits at some point."

Janina Söhn of the Institute for Sociological Research (SOFI) at Göttingen University has also studied the issue of poverty among older immigrants in Germany.

It's a major problem in Germany that nearly one-third of immigrants are at risk of poverty, she said.

"This group faces even greater hardship than, for example, women in general, who already have a higher risk of poverty. And when you then look specifically at female migrants living alone, the figures are truly dire and alarming. If there were no family support, it would be an even sorrier situation."

Older Turkish migrants in Germany also often have limited opportunities to earn extra euros during retirement.

This is because either because they are poorly qualified or because the hard physical labor they performed when they were younger has left them physically unfit.

According to figures from Germany's Federal Employment Agency, the employment rate of for retired Turkish people living in Germany is only half that of Germans (5.2% compared to 10.8%).

"Basically, they face a whole series of disadvantages or hardships in life. That generation of guest workers was brought to Germany and then had to do the worst jobs here, whereas many Germans were able to progress through education and training," Söhn said.

The Turkish workers in Germany didn't get similar chances.

"The people who did these tough jobs, which are always necessary for any economy, paid for it with their health," she said.

This article was originally written in German.

#658. Scientists discover a bacterial defense so strange they thought it was broken

Scientists at Gladstone Institutes have discovered an unusual bacterial immune system that operates in almost the opposite way of previously known defenses. The surprising mechanism allows bacteria to activate a deadly self-destruct process when viruses attack, potentially offering new ideas for developing medical treatments and gene-editing technologies.

The findings, published in Molecular Cell, reveal how a group of bacterial defense systems called "type VI retrons" use an unexpectedly complex sequence of molecular events to fight infection. Unlike other retrons, these systems rely on DNA to activate a toxin rather than keep one suppressed.

Understanding this unusual process could do more than expand scientists' knowledge of bacterial immunity. It may also provide a foundation for designing more effective DNA-editing tools, potentially allowing researchers to correct harmful genetic mutations with greater precision.

"This is, by far, the strangest of the retron systems that we or anyone else has come across," says Gladstone Investigator Seth Shipman, PhD, senior author of the new study. "These retrons operate with Rube Goldberg-level complexity, using molecular mechanisms that we would never have thought to invent, but that we'll use in future technologies."

How Bacteria Sacrifice Themselves to Stop Viruses

Bacteria face constant threats from viruses known as phages, which infect bacterial cells and use their machinery to reproduce. Over time, bacteria have evolved a variety of defenses to prevent these viruses from spreading.

Among these defenses are retrons, molecular systems that can detect certain viral infections and trigger the infected bacterium to destroy itself. Although this sacrifice kills the individual cell, it prevents the virus from producing more copies and infecting nearby bacteria, helping protect the larger colony.

Retrons are also of considerable interest to scientists developing new genetic technologies. They can efficiently produce and deliver single-stranded DNA, making them promising tools for editing DNA inside human cells. Shipman's team and other researchers are investigating whether these capabilities could eventually be used to correct mutations responsible for disease with exceptional accuracy.

Until now, scientists believed they understood the basic way retron defenses operate.

In previously studied retrons, a toxic protein is already present inside an uninfected cell, but its harmful effects are held in check by short pieces of single-stranded DNA. When a phage infects the bacterium, it disrupts this protective arrangement, allowing the toxin to act. The resulting cell death prevents the virus from spreading.

The newly investigated type VI retrons, however, did not appear to follow this familiar pattern.

A Bacterial Immune System That Works Backward

Researchers first became suspicious that type VI retrons were different when they could not detect the single-stranded DNA normally associated with these systems.

"The way we typically detect retrons inside uninfected cells is by looking for this single-stranded DNA," says Karen Zhang, a PhD student in Shipman's lab and lead author of the study. "But type VI retrons caught our attention because they didn't appear to have this signature. It was very odd, and we wondered if they might be broken."

Despite their unusual behavior, experiments showed that bacteria carrying type VI retrons could still defend themselves against phage infections. The systems were clearly functional, even though they lacked the expected molecular signs of activity.

"That kicked off a long molecular odyssey," Shipman says. "Whenever we tried the experiments we normally use to study retrons, they would fail, so we kept having to think of new ways to figure out how these retrons work."

After extensive investigation, the team discovered that type VI retrons reverse a key step in the usual defense process.

Rather than maintaining a substantial supply of single-stranded DNA and toxin before infection, these retrons produce little detectable DNA and no noticeable amount of toxin in healthy cells. The arrival of a phage triggers a sharp increase in DNA production.

As the DNA accumulates, it interacts with an RNA molecule that has been preventing the toxin from being made. This interaction removes the restriction, allowing the bacterium to rapidly produce the toxic protein.

The toxin appears to be an exceptionally small protein that inserts itself into the bacterium's surrounding cell membrane. By disrupting the membrane's stability, it causes the infected cell to die, stopping the viral infection from spreading.

In other words, the DNA acts as an activation switch rather than a restraint. Instead of preventing an existing toxin from causing harm, it helps turn on toxin production only when the bacterium detects a threat.

"It's almost the mirror-image version of how we traditionally view retrons, because the DNA switches on toxin production instead of inhibiting an already-produced toxin," Zhang says. "It would be fascinating to explore how bacterial evolution could have resulted in such a complex molecular system -- whether type VI retrons are older or newer than other retrons, or whether they're a stepping stone between different types."

An Unusual Discovery Required New Experiments

Figuring out how type VI retrons function proved unusually difficult. Many established techniques that scientists use to examine retrons repeatedly produced no useful results, forcing the team to develop new experimental strategies and adapt existing methods.

One particularly important challenge involved detecting the DNA produced by type VI retrons in cells that had not been infected.

After conventional tests failed, the researchers tried a technique called Spacer-seq, which had previously been developed in Shipman's laboratory. The method uses components of CRISPR-Cas, another bacterial immune system, to record molecular activity inside cells.

CRISPR-Cas is best known for its role in modern gene-editing technologies, but bacteria originally evolved these systems as defenses against viruses. Spacer-seq takes advantage of this natural machinery to help researchers investigate what happens inside cells.

The alternative approach finally revealed a trace amount of single-stranded DNA that earlier experiments had missed.

"We had just about given up hope that any DNA was being made when this approach finally revealed a very, very low level of production in uninfected cells," Zhang says.

This breakthrough encouraged the researchers to continue investigating. Additional experiments confirmed that type VI retrons produce DNA at very low levels under normal conditions and substantially increase production only after a phage enters the cell.

The findings explained why the defense system had appeared inactive in earlier tests and revealed the unusual sequence of events responsible for its antiviral activity.

Could This Strange Bacterial Defense Lead to New Medical Treatments?

The discovery is already influencing research in Shipman's laboratory, where scientists are exploring ways to transform the type VI retron's natural machinery into useful technologies.

One promising application involves developing synthetic molecular sensors and switches that can regulate gene activity. Such systems could potentially allow researchers to control when particular genes are activated or suppressed, opening new possibilities for studying disease and designing treatments.

"This system represents a unique way to potentially build a molecular sensor and switch encoded in DNA and RNA, that no one has thought of before," Zhang says. "Synthetic sensors and switches have many possible applications, both in treating disease and in designing experiments to better understand how certain diseases operate."

Another possibility involves the retron's unusually small but powerful toxins. Because these proteins can disrupt bacterial membranes and kill cells, researchers are investigating whether they could be adapted into new antimicrobial treatments.

Such therapies could potentially target harmful bacteria responsible for human infections, providing a new approach to combating bacterial disease.

These medical applications remain under development, but the discovery offers researchers a molecular design that would have been difficult to imagine without studying nature's existing solutions.

"This study highlights why it's so important for a molecular technology development lab like ours to keep looking to nature for inspiration," Shipman says. "We can use what evolution has given us as starting points to build complex machines that would have been tremendously hard to even conceptualize."

The research also raises intriguing questions about bacterial evolution, including how such an elaborate defense arose and whether type VI retrons represent an earlier, later, or intermediate stage in the evolution of these immune systems.

For scientists seeking new ways to manipulate DNA, control genes, and fight infections, this backward-acting bacterial defense could provide an unexpected starting point.

The research, "Reverse transcribed ssDNA derepresses translation of a retron antiviral protein," was published in Molecular Cell on October 13, 2026.

Along with Shipman and Zhang, the authors include Matías Rojas-Montero, Darshini Poola, and Alejandro González-Delgado of Gladstone; Josepha Klas, Arturo Carabias, Dennis Zhang, Mario Mestre, Ruiliang Zhao, Ana Dávila-Hidalgo, Guillermo Montoya, and Rafael Pinilla-Redondo of the University of Copenhagen; and Lieza Chan and Kliment Verba of UC San Francisco.

The research received support from the National Science Foundation, the Robert J. Kleeberg Jr. and Helen C. Kleberg Foundation, the Gordon and Betty Moore Foundation, the Lundbeck Foundation, the Fulbright U.S. Student Program, the Junta de Castilla y León and European Social Fund Plus, the European Molecular Biology Organization, the Novo Nordisk Foundation, the European Research Council, and the Villum Foundation.

On Nov. 3, 1957, a Soviet space dog named Laika became the first animal to orbit Earth.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

On Nov. 3, 1957, a Soviet space dog named Laika became the first animal to orbit Earth. Laika was a 3-year-old stray husky-spitz mix from the streets of Moscow, and she was recruited by the Soviet space program for her small size and calm temperament.

Unfortunately for Laika, this mission was a one-way trip. The Soviets didn't design a way to bring her back down to Earth. With only 7 days worth of oxygen and a little bit of food on board, Laika launched from the Baikonur Cosmodrome in Kazakhstan with a Russian Sputnik rocket. This was the same kind of rocket used to launch the first Sputnik satellite.

Laika was alive when she reached orbit, but she died shortly afterward because the spacecraft's heat shield had broken off. Laika overheated before she had the chance to die of starvation of oxygen deprivation.

Laika has remained one of space history's most beloved and tragic figures. People around the world have dogs as pets who they love as members of their own families. And even nearly 70 years after this flight, it is so heartbreaking to think of Laika on that frightening journey from which she never returned.

Laika was one of many different animals that were used in early spaceflight testing. Both the U.S. and Russia launched a number of primates on flights testing early flight technology. Sadly, like Laika, many of these brave creatures did not make it back.

Unbelievably, though, some did survive the journey. For example, the chimpanzee named Ham and nicknamed the "astrochimp" survived a 1961 test flight to space. Though, the team behind that flight was so unsure of how it would go that Ham didn't get his name until after it was found that he'd survived his return.

Want more space history? Check out our full On This Day In Space Story archive and watch our On This Day In Space videos on YouTube.

After studying physics at the University of Tennessee in her hometown of Knoxville, she earned her graduate degree in Science, Health and Environmental Reporting (SHERP) from New York University. In her spare time, Hanneke enjoys exploring the Rocky Mountains, basking in nature and looking for dark skies to gaze at the cosmos.

#656. Moon phase today: What the Moon will look like on November 4, 2026

The Moon is currently in its waning phase, meaning the illuminated portion we can see from Earth is gradually getting smaller. As it moves through the Waning Crescent stage, only a small sliver remains visible before the Moon reaches its New Moon phase.

As of Wednesday, Nov. 3, NASA's Daily Moon Guide tracker tells us the Moon is in the Waning Crescent phase, with 25% of its surface visible.

Tonight, without the use of visual aids you should be able to spot the Aristarchus Plateau and that's all. With binoculars or a telescope, you'll be able to see this and the Kepler Crater.

The next Full Moon will take place on November 24.

It takes the Moon around 29.5 days to pass through a complete lunar cycle. As it travels around Earth, the angle at which sunlight reaches its surface changes what we can see from here, producing the different phases, from the New Moon through to the Full Moon and back again. The cycle then starts over, as explained by NASA.

New Moon - The Moon is between Earth and the sun, so the side we see is dark (in other words, it's invisible to the eye).

Waxing Crescent - A small sliver of light appears on the right side (Northern Hemisphere).

First Quarter - Half of the Moon is lit on the right side. It looks like a half-Moon.

Waxing Gibbous - More than half is lit up, but it's not quite full yet.

Full Moon - The whole face of the Moon is illuminated and fully visible.

Waning Gibbous - The Moon starts losing light on the right side. (Northern Hemisphere)

Third Quarter (or Last Quarter) - Another half-Moon, but now the left side is lit.

Waning Crescent - A thin sliver of light remains on the left side before going dark again.

Lois Mackenzie is a freelance reporter at Mashable. Over the years she has written for many publications, covering everything from the local news to the best pair of running shoes. You can find bylines in publications including Fit&Well, Metro, and Coach magazine, usually covering deals on everything from earbuds to TVs, or guides on how to beat your half marathon time.

Lois also holds a Master's degree in Digital Journalism from Strathclyde University and obtained a Master of Arts in English Literature at the University of Aberdeen.

#655. 75,000-year-old Neanderthal may have been killed by a spear aimed at the heart

A small, circular hole in a 75,000-year-old Neanderthal shoulder blade may reveal one of the earliest known cases of deadly violence involving a wooden spear. The remarkable discovery, made in a cave in Iraqi Kurdistan, suggests that the individual was struck by a sharpened wooden weapon that passed through the chest, potentially in a deliberate attack aimed at the heart.

Researchers believe the wound could represent the oldest evidence in the hominin fossil record of fatal interpersonal violence involving a wooden spear.

The shoulder blade (scapula) is an unusually delicate bone, with some areas so thin that light can pass through them. Despite its fragile structure, the Neanderthal's bone survived for approximately 75,000 years beneath seven and a half meters of rock and sediment. Almost the entire bone remained intact, except for a remarkably precise circular opening measuring 15 millimeters across.

A Deadly Spear Wound Reveals a Neanderthal's Violent Death

Archaeologists from the University of Cambridge, who led the excavation, believe the hole was created by a spear with a sharpened wooden point. Its rounded shape is an important clue because weapons tipped with flint or stone generally produce openings with flatter or more angular edges.

Their reconstruction suggests that the spear entered the front of the Neanderthal's left chest, passed through a lung and probably major blood vessels, and continued until it pierced the shoulder blade from behind. Such a severe injury would have caused rapid death. The researchers suspect the blow may have been an intentional "heart shot."

The physical evidence offers additional clues about how the attack occurred. The opening has beveled edges, a feature commonly associated with an exit wound. Small bone fragments displaced during the impact indicate that the weapon likely entered from above and traveled downward through the body.

Using these fragments, the scientists were able to partially reconstruct the damaged area. Subtle ridges left by muscle attachments helped them determine where the pieces originally belonged.

"It's extraordinary to have a perfectly preserved scapula from 75,000 years ago. These bones are so thin that you often don't get complete scapulae from modern burials," said Dr. Emma Pomeroy, study lead author from Cambridge's Department of Archaeology. "We were able to lift it out in one piece from under almost eight meters of rock and sediment."

The remains have been named Shanidar A after the cave where they were uncovered. The findings were published in the journal Scientific Reports.

Ancient Wooden Spears Were Sophisticated Hunting Weapons

Although sharpened wooden weapons were used hundreds of thousands of years ago, relatively few examples have survived. Wood usually decays over time, making it exceptionally difficult for archaeologists to recover evidence of ancient woodworking and weapon technology.

One important discovery occurred in the 1990s at Schöningen, Germany, where researchers uncovered wooden spears preserved in waterlogged conditions. Dating back roughly 200,000 years, these weapons were made during a period when early Neanderthals inhabited Europe.

Some measured more than two meters in length. Their makers carefully selected the wood and shaped the spears to achieve a balance suitable for throwing, much like modern javelins. Archaeologists believe they were probably used to hunt large animals.

Even older evidence comes from Clacton-on-Sea in the United Kingdom. In 1911, a pointed wooden fragment was recovered from the shoreline and later identified as part of a spear more than 400,000 years old. Only its tip had survived, making it the earliest known example of a rounded wooden spear.

The Cambridge researchers believe comparable weapons could have been responsible for Shanidar A's death. If their interpretation is correct, the injury may provide the first evidence that sharpened wooden spears were used in the prehistoric Middle East.

"Holes left by recreations of spears from this time are an excellent fit for the one we found in the Neanderthal scapula," said Pomeroy, a fellow at Newnham College, Cambridge. "That early technology absolutely works for this wound."

"What evidence we have suggests that Neanderthals and their ancestors developed woodworking and weapon-making skills many thousands of years before the death of Shanidar A. This package of capabilities could have spanned the full range of Neanderthal homelands, from Wales to Siberia."

The discovery raises a difficult question: Was Shanidar A the victim of a deliberate attack, or did a hunting accident cause the fatal injury?

Pomeroy acknowledges that accidents involving wooden spears would have been possible, particularly when Neanderthals hunted large, dangerous animals at close range.

"Animals such as mammoths may have been hunted up close with thrusting spears, so it's easy to imagine lethal injuries."

Nevertheless, certain features of the wound suggest that the blow may have been intentional rather than accidental.

"The position of the wound and the force required to push it right through the Neanderthal's body bear the hallmarks of an intended kill shot directed towards the heart."

The researchers cannot determine exactly what happened or who wielded the weapon. It is also impossible to establish whether modern humans played any role. However, they consider violence between Neanderthals the simplest explanation consistent with the available evidence.

"All we can ever know about the end of this Neanderthal's life is that it was violent, and came at the end of a wooden spear," said Prof Graeme Barker, fellow of St. John's College, Cambridge, who leads the Shanidar Cave excavations.

"Evidence of systematic violence is extremely rare in deep prehistory. The vast majority comes from periods of settled farming communities thousands of years after hunter-gather societies like our Neanderthals."

A Shattered Tooth Reveals a Surprising Story of Compassion

Although Shanidar A appears to have died violently, other evidence suggests this individual received considerable care earlier in life.

Alongside the shoulder blade, archaeologists recovered a nearly complete right hand, two ribs from the left side, a fragment of a right rib, and seven teeth. Together, these are the surviving remains of an adult Neanderthal believed to have been approximately 45 years old at death.

One tooth provides particularly revealing evidence about the individual's life. An incisor from the front of the lower jaw had been split vertically, leaving just half of the tooth intact. Neighboring teeth had also been forced inward.

Researchers believe the damage resulted from a powerful blow to the face. The surviving half of the incisor had accumulated substantial tartar (dental calculus) along its exposed root canal, indicating that the damaged tooth remained in the mouth for an extended period after the injury.

This buildup suggests that Shanidar A survived the original trauma rather than dying immediately. Such extensive facial damage would likely have made eating and communicating extremely painful and difficult.

"Surviving a blow that splits a tooth in this fashion, then continuing to live and eat for a period of at least a year and maybe more, would have required care and support from other Neanderthals," said Pomeroy.

The researchers suggest that other members of the group may have helped Shanidar A survive by providing softer foods. Earlier studies of sediments from Shanidar Cave found evidence that Neanderthals were soaking plant foods before cooking them around this period.

This method of food preparation could have made meals easier for someone suffering from severe facial injuries.

"There's no doubt that Shanidar A would have had difficulty communicating and been in absolute agony for a long period of time."

For the scientists, these findings reveal two seemingly opposite aspects of Neanderthal behavior in the life of a single individual.

"The remains of Shanidar A reflect the dual nature of so much of what we recognize as human. On the one hand, we have evidence of a terribly violent end. On the other, this was clearly an individual who was cared for during their lifetime."

Prof Barker said: "It is fascinating to have evidence for both compassion and violence amongst Neanderthals, our closest evolutionary cousins, embodied in this one individual."

Shanidar Cave Is Transforming Our Understanding of Neanderthals

Shanidar Cave, situated in the foothills of Iraqi Kurdistan, has played a major role in changing scientific views of Neanderthal behavior.

During the 1950s, excavations led by archaeologist Ralph Solecki uncovered the remains of ten Neanderthals. Four individuals were found grouped together in the same location, even though they had died at different times.

Their placement suggested that Neanderthals may have repeatedly returned to a particular part of the cave to bury their dead.

Another remarkable discovery from a different section of the cave involved a Neanderthal who lived thousands of years later. This individual had experienced serious physical disabilities, including a paralyzed arm, arthritis, hearing loss, and partial blindness.

Despite these conditions, the individual survived to an advanced age, suggesting that other members of the community provided assistance and care.

Discoveries like these helped overturn the image of Neanderthals that prevailed during the Victorian era, when they were often portrayed as primitive, brutish, and less than fully human.

Subsequent research has revealed increasingly sophisticated behavior, including cave art and jewelry. Genetic studies have also established that Neanderthals interbred with modern humans, leaving traces of their DNA in populations alive today.

Evidence Suggests Neanderthals Returned to Bury Their Dead

Shanidar A, excavated in 2020, adds another important piece to this growing picture of Neanderthal society.

Since 2015, the Cambridge-led archaeological team has identified three additional Neanderthals within the cave's previously known cluster of remains. These discoveries bring the number of individuals in that particular burial area to five, consisting of four adults and one infant.

All five were found within an extraordinarily confined space measuring approximately 1.5 meters long, one meter wide, and one meter deep.

The location lies immediately behind a large upright boulder that researchers describe as a "prominent marker." Thin layers of sediment separate the individual sets of remains, indicating that the bodies were deposited at different times.

Shanidar A was discovered at the greatest depth within the cluster and may have been the first individual placed there. The body was positioned on its back, with the head pointing east. The Neanderthal found directly above it had been arranged in a similar position.

These patterns suggest that the cave's occupants were not simply leaving bodies wherever space was available. Instead, they may have deliberately chosen a particular location and returned to it repeatedly to lay deceased members of their community to rest.

"The best explanation is intentional and symbolic funerary behavior," said Pomeroy. "These Neanderthals returned to the same place to lay their dead to rest. Some were deposited before the earlier body had fully decomposed, so this was happening within years or decades."

Taken together, the discoveries at Shanidar Cave paint a complex picture of Neanderthal life 75,000 years ago. The same individual who may have died in a deliberate spear attack had apparently survived a devastating earlier injury with the help of others and was eventually placed in a location that may have held special significance for the community.

Far from fitting the outdated stereotype of Neanderthals as simple, brutal creatures, Shanidar A provides rare physical evidence of a society capable of both deadly violence and sustained compassion.
